sources.headline: Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election
sources.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's decision to call a snap election for 29 November came on the back of a parliamentary defeat. On Friday, the raft of measures he had presented to congress aimed at improving conditions for tenants and trying to address the problem of soaring rentals was narrowly rejected, as parties on the right voted against them.That parliamentary result confirmed that Sánchez's left-wing coalition no longer commanded a majority. But as has so often been the case throughout Sánchez's career, the calling of the election was not a knee-jerk reaction but a carefully thought-out manouevre.His government has been struggling in recent months. His Socialist Party has been mired in corruption, with cases implicating former senior figures in the party, Santos Cerdán and José Luis Ábalos, while the former Socialist Prime Minister, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, is facing accusations of having benefited financially from the government's bailout of an airline. Zapatero has denied wrongdoing.In addition, Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, is due to go on trial over allegations of misuse of funds and influence peddling - accusations that Gómez and Sánchez vehemently deny.Meanwhile, Sánchez's administration has struggled to manage the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, where more than 70,000 migrants suddenly arrived in July. Most have returned over the border to Morocco, but the city has become a political and logistical headache for the prime minister.The PP and Vox tend to oppose any initiative presented by the Sánchez government, which they have long cast as illegitimate due to its scandals and reliance on Catalan and Basque nationalists. However, as a matter of policy, parties on the right tend to oppose the kind of direct intervention in the housing market that Sánchez has been advocating, warning that it can be counterproductive.Earlier this year, when Sánchez's international profile rose due to his outspoken criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and his clashes with US President Donald Trump, there was speculation that he might have used the political capital that gave him on the left and called an early election back then. However, the housing issue, which is the biggest concern for Spaniards according to polls, appears more likely to mobilise support on the left.Yet polls also show that the Socialists are trailing the PP. While the housing issue provides Sánchez with a potential fillip on the campaign trail, staying in power after these elections will be probably the biggest challenge of his career.

sources.headline: Spain calls snap election amid housing crisis
Spain’s Leader Calls an Early Election
Sanchez chose 'best moment in a sea of troubles' to call for snap election, analyst says
When growth is not enough: housing and inflation, Sánchez's key election challenges
sources.text:
The President of the Spanish Government, Pedro Sánchez, will face the snap elections on 29 November hoping that the strong economic figures that have marked much of his time in office will help him overcome a widespread feeling across the country: macro-level growth is not enough.
Spain's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 2.8% in 2025 and is expected to continue expanding at a relatively brisk pace, with growth forecast at 2.4% for 2026, as the European Commission's country report on Spain points out (source in Spanish). Since the pandemic, moreover, Spain has grown faster than the main economies of the euro area.
However, as the protests over the housing crisis that have gripped the country for weeks make clear, that growth has not translated into an improvement in Spaniards' quality of life. The Commission attributes part of this to a sharp increase in the population, driven by migration flows, but also to weak labour productivity.
Hourly productivity has improved since 2019, but productivity per employee and per full-time worker has remained virtually flat. That is one of the main reasons why aggregate growth is not being reflected to the same extent in per capita income in a Spain that Sánchez has governed since June 2018.
Immigration, in fact, has become one of the engines of the Spanish labour market. While employment grew by 2.6% in 2025, the number of jobs filled by people born abroad accounted for 7.9% of all the posts created that year.
The latest consolidated figures nevertheless show that the labour market still has a strongly seasonal pattern. In August, unemployment rose by 44,419 people, to 2,355,918, although this was the lowest figure recorded in that month since 2007. In September, the jobless total increased again, by 23,587 people, which was also a low for that month since 2007.
The main pillar of Spanish growth has been the services sector, and specifically exports of services and tourism. Spain received 58.1 million international tourists between January and July 2026, an unprecedented figure and 4.6% more than a year earlier. Tourist spending rose by 7.8%, reaching a record 82.054 billion euros, according to the Frontur and Egatur data published (source in Spanish) by the National Statistics Institute (INE).
The European Commission stresses that the increase in exported services has helped widen the current account surplus and improve the country's international investment position. But it also warns that a significant share of activity remains concentrated in sectors with relatively low productivity, such as agriculture. More than 82% of the jobs created were in low-productivity activities, limiting the scope for wage growth.
Inflation adds another layer of tension. In September, annual inflation in the country stood at 5%, well above the 3.8% recorded on average in the euro area, and only behind Lithuania (6.1%), Bulgaria (5.6%), Cyprus and Luxembourg (5.2%) and Greece (5.1%).
In September, inflation in Spain stood at 4.9%. The INE mainly attributed the Spanish spike to rising fuel prices and the behaviour of package holidays.
Housing, the big problem
If there is one issue that sums up the imbalance between economic growth and quality of life, it is housing. Here, Spain faces a serious mismatch between supply and demand, both for buying and renting, especially in large cities and tourist areas.
"The severe rate of housing deprivation increased, which indicates poor living conditions", says the Commission's country report. Social housing accounts for barely between 1.5% and 1.7% of the total stock, compared with an average of between 6% and 7% in the European Union.
On top of that, prices have been rising steadily since 2014 and have accelerated in recent years, while high costs are also making labour mobility more difficult.
This is precisely where the economy and politics collided on Monday. After the Government failed to ratify two decrees last week to tackle the housing crisis because it lacked the support of its partners in Congress, Prime Minister Sánchez dissolved parliament and called elections for November.
Thus, the economic balance sheet of Sánchez's term in office so far has two sides: one in which Spain is growing, creating jobs and benefiting from the arrival of foreign workers and the strength of the tourism sector; and another, which GDP growth alone cannot solve, weighed down by low productivity, the loss of purchasing power and the difficulty of accessing housing.

sources.headline: Spain's prime minister calls early elections as pressure mounts over housing crisis
sources.text:
People seen through a window inside a bar in La Cabrera, on the outskirts of Madrid, Spain, watch a televised speech by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez from La Moncloa Palace announcing national elections, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026.
Bernat Armangue/AP
hide caption
Bernat Armangue/AP
MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced early elections Monday after his government suffered a bruising legislative defeat last week on emergency measures related to the country's housing crisis.
The vote will be held Nov. 29. In recent weeks, Spaniards have demanded solutions from the government over housing affordability, holding protests in cities across the country after public outrage grew over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid last month. Right-wing opposition parties joined forces to scuttle two emergency decrees in Parliament that included measures to reduce evictions and real estate speculation. The setback sparked wide speculation that Sánchez could consider moving up a national election that would have otherwise taken place next year.
In a televised address, Sánchez argued that a broader progressive coalition in Parliament would allow Spaniards to tackle the biggest issues facing the country today. "The time has come, therefore, for the Spanish people to decide what future you want for yourselves and for your country," Sánchez said. Sánchez, 54, has been Spain's prime minister since 2018, making him one of Europe's longest-standing leaders. He has become one of the leading international progressive heads of government thanks to his defense of migration, his diplomatic efforts to defend Palestinians and his criticism of the American and Israeli war against Iran. He has also enjoyed one of the fastest growing economies in the developed world in recent years.
But back home, the Spanish leader has been hemmed in by a series of legal cases involving his Socialist party as well as his wife and brother, who both deny wrongdoing. He has also struggled to account for this summer's border crossing by tens of thousands of mostly Moroccans into Spain's North African territory of Ceuta, where a humanitarian crisis remains two months after the initial crisis. He has led a coalition minority government along with the left-wing junior partner Sumar since 2023. But his reliance on several smaller parties to get anything done has hamstrung his legislative ability.
Throughout his political career, Sánchez has earned a reputation as a political escape artist capable of winning elections he looked set to lose. Speculation around whether he would call snap elections centered on the momentum that his party may now have around issues of affordability, while the opposition Popular Party — which holds the most seats in Parliament already — is likely to define the contest around corruption. "Sánchez is choosing this moment because it is arguably the best time to do so, given that the issue of housing frames the electoral conflict or debate in terms that are highly favorable to (his party's) position," said Oriol Bartomeus, a professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. "Sánchez can frame the election — or has realized he can frame it — in very classic left-versus-right terms," Bartomeus said." The Socialist leader will face Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who aims to take control of the government. "At last, the Spanish people will decide," Feijóo said Monday after the announcement of the the snap election. "These aren't elections like the previous ones. This is about Spain beating Sánchez," he said. The formal dissolution of parliament will need to be approved by the Cabinet, which Sánchez has convened for later Monday.

sources.headline: Spain's gambler PM Sanchez seeks to defy the odds again on a snap election
sources.text: MADRID, Oct 5 - Spain's Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, on Monday lived up to his reputation as a political gambler by calling a snap election that surveys indicate will cost him his job and usher in a right-wing government.But then, the 54-year-old has managed to remain in office for eight years without ever winning a majority in parliament.His appetite for risk has led him to openly accuse Israel of genocide in Gaza, a charge it rejects, and to defy US President Donald Trump's demands that Madrid spend much more on defence and let the US use its airbases in Spain for its war on Iran.His latest gamble - to bring the election forward to November 29 from next year - appears to be based on a calculation that anger over a mounting housing crisis will be directed more at his opponents than at his own party.SANCHEZ AIMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF HOUSING CRISISOn Friday, his right-wing opponents blocked his attempt to answer protesters' anger over the eviction of 87-year-old tenant Maricarmen Abascal with a decree capping rents and blocking further evictions.With thousands of activists camped in the capital outside the office of the Madrid regional government, led by the conservative People's Party, Sanchez could be trying to make the election a referendum on housing.It could also shift the narrative from damaging headlines about his government's handling of a migrant crisis in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta this summer, and investigations into alleged corruption in his party and influence peddling by his wife and brother. Anger still lingers, too, at an amnesty for Catalan separatists that allowed him to clinch a third term in 2023."Faced with an inability to legislate on the issue of greatest public concern, the aim is to capitalise on social mobilisation," said political analyst Eduardo Bayon."The logic is to transform a tangible problem into a choice between political blocs: 'This is what I am trying to do, but the right-wing parties are blocking me'."Surveys indicate the housing measures rejected by the PP, Vox and the Catalan nationalists Junts have support across Spanish society. A 40dB survey for El Pais and Cadena Ser on Friday found that 68% of Spaniards, including a majority of PP and Vox voters, were in favour of capping rents to make housing more accessible."In contrast to their (opposition parties') penthouses, their budget cuts and their subservience to the elites, our pledge to the people is for affordable housing, public services and social rights," Sanchez wrote on X on Monday. "Spain must continue to move forward, and to do so, we need the public to strengthen our position in parliament."SANCHEZ ALWAYS DEFYING THE ODDSSanchez has defied the odds throughout his political career. He first grabbed power by leading a move to remove his conservative predecessor, Mariano Rajoy of the PP, in Spain's first successful no-confidence vote over corruption.In two subsequent elections, he has mobilised his base by pitching himself as a progressive bulwark against the far right returning to power for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco's 36-year right-wing dictatorship in 1975.In 2023, he called a snap election after the Socialists performed badly in local ballots. It paid off: With no political party prepared to endorse Vox, Sanchez cobbled together an eclectic alliance to back him for a third term, even though the PP had won the most seats.Still, the chances of that happening look even slimmer than in 2023, with support for the Socialists and their minority coalition partners Sumar well below what it was then.Sanchez could also be playing a long game, betting that, even if he does not win, he can wait in the wings as an effective opposition leader, said Lorenzo Bernaldo de Quiros, an economist and president of the consultancy Freemarket Corporate Intelligence.Sanchez's Socialists are betting that, although a PP-Vox coalition government is now a possibility, it would be beset by policy conflicts, which has been the case in the four regional governments where the PP and Vox currently rule in coalition."It is a government that (the Socialists) believe will not last," Bernaldo de Quiros said. REUTERS
